statement: In people who take MDMA, evidence is insufficient to say how often passing urine becomes difficult, or why: no study read here measured difficulty passing urine, the amount of urine passed or how the bladder worked after MDMA, and the only report read of someone unable to pass urine is a single case. In that case, a healthy 19-year-old man was referred to a hospital urology team in the UK after 24 hours of acute retention of urine: apart from a painful bladder that could be felt, examination and a routine urine test were normal; a catheter drained the bladder and was removed after 36 hours, and the retention did not come back (how long he was followed is not stated). By his own account he had used only ecstasy in the previous 12 months, one or two tablets once or twice a week, usually at parties, and he later said he had taken 15 tablets in the 36 hours before admission (as reported, not a recommendation); neither he nor the tablets were tested for any drug, and when he took the last tablet is not given. His doctors wrote that the drug had 'almost certainly' caused the retention, reasoning that MDMA stimulates the alpha-adrenergic nerve fibres that can close the bladder neck; nothing was measured in him to test this, no other cause was looked for beyond the examination, and the only earlier urinary complication they knew of was an urgent need to pass urine (second-hand, from a 1986 report) (Bryden et al., 1995). The controlled studies read measured the body's water balance, not passing urine. In 8 healthy men aged 22 to 32 given one capsule of MDMA (47.5 mg of the hydrochloride, equal to 40 mg of MDMA base, with 200 mL of water; study conditions), antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin), the hormone that tells the body to hold back water, peaked 1 to 2 hours later, from a range of 1.14 to 1.88 pmol/L before the dose to 2.46 to 9.16 pmol/L at 2 hours (one-tailed p = 0.006), and blood sodium fell by 1 to 3 mmol/L in 7 of the 8 (one-tailed p = 0.025); the only comparison was 3 of the same men on a later, untreated occasion, not compared statistically, and no urine was measured (Henry et al., 1998). In two double-blind studies in which healthy people who had taken MDMA before had MDMA (1.5 mg/kg of the hydrochloride; study condition) and a placebo on different days (Baggott et al., 2016), MDMA did not raise the hormone in 16 people whose drinking was limited to about 473 mL an hour (z = 1.21, p = 0.589), while prazosin, a medicine that lowers blood pressure, given as a check because it releases the hormone, did; and in 12 people who drank 20 mL/kg of water an hour after the capsule, neither the hormone (p = 0.74) nor copeptin, a marker released with it (p = 0.89), rose. In a third double-blind crossover study, of 32 healthy volunteers given 125 mg (study condition), copeptin measured before and 1 and 2 hours after the dose did not change (no statistic printed; Hysek et al., 2014). Blood sodium did fall after MDMA in Baggott's studies: by less than 2 mmol/L at its lowest against placebo when drinking was limited, and further after the water load than after the same water load with placebo (lowest value, F(1,9) = 13.2, p = 0.005; means about 133.6 against 137.7 mmol/L at 3 hours; both editors' approximate readings of the paper's figures), with one woman reaching 127 mmol/L without symptoms; two people who vomited soon after drinking the water in their MDMA session were left out. The authors could not explain the fall by the hormone, copeptin or drug levels, and did not establish a mechanism. They collected urine before the dose and over 0 to 8 and 8 to 24 hours after it, but report no urine result, and list not measuring urine concentration (osmolality) as a limitation. All these volunteers were healthy and took a single known dose given by researchers in a research setting. Where a larger fall in blood sodium can lead (seizures, brain swelling and deaths, reported mostly in young people) is a separate answer (see the answer on whether drinking lots of water on MDMA can lead to low blood salt). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Why is it hard to pee on MDMA? Nobody knows for sure, because no study has measured it. Studies measured the body's water-holding hormone instead. It rose 1 to 2 hours after one capsule of MDMA in a study of 8 healthy men, but that study had no proper comparison, and three better-controlled studies, in which the same people took MDMA on one day and a dummy pill on another, found no rise in the hormone or in a marker released with it. Blood salt did fall a little after MDMA, and more when people drank a lot of water; a bigger fall in blood salt is covered in a separate answer. The team that found this collected urine but never reported what it found. The only case in these papers of someone who couldn't pee at all is one 19-year-old man in the UK in 1995: he couldn't pass urine for 24 hours after saying he had taken 15 ecstasy tablets in 36 hours, and a tube drained his bladder. Nobody tested him or the tablets for drugs, and his doctors' explanation, that MDMA tightens the outlet of the bladder, was their reasoning, not a measurement.
population: People who take MDMA: one healthy 19-year-old man treated by a hospital urology team in the UK (case report); in laboratory studies, 8 healthy men aged 22 to 32 in London (Henry et al., 1998), 16 people (8 women, 8 men; aged 18 to 42) and 12 people (6 women, 6 men; aged 21 to 40) in the USA, all healthy and with earlier MDMA use (Baggott et al., 2016), and 32 healthy volunteers in Basel (16 women, 16 men; aged 20 to 31; 22 had never taken MDMA) (Hysek et al., 2014)
exposure: MDMA: in the case, tablets sold as ecstasy, 15 in the 36 hours before admission by the man's own account, content untested (as reported, not a recommendation); in the laboratory, a single oral dose given by researchers (study conditions): 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride (40 mg base) with 200 mL of water (Henry), 1.5 mg/kg MDMA hydrochloride with drinking limited to about 473 mL an hour or followed an hour later by 20 mL/kg of water drunk within 30 minutes (Baggott), or 125 mg (Hysek)
comparator: None in the case report; each man's own values before the dose, and 3 of the men on a later untreated occasion, not compared statistically (Henry); placebo in the same people on another day, double-blind (Baggott, Hysek), with prazosin as a check drug in Baggott's first study and the same water load after placebo in the second
outcome: Difficulty passing urine, urine volume and bladder function (not measured in any study read; one case of acute retention of urine described); antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) and copeptin; blood sodium
magnitude: Bryden et al. (1995), one case: man aged 19; acute retention for 24 hours before referral; painful palpable bladder; examination and urinalysis otherwise normal; urethral catheter removed after 36 hours on free drainage; no further retention (follow-up length not stated); self-reported use: only ecstasy in the previous 12 months, one or two tablets once or twice a week, then 15 tablets in the 36 hours before admission (earlier amphetamine and cannabis); no drug screen, no tablet analysis, no residual volume, flow study or imaging. Henry et al. (1998), 8 healthy men aged 22-32, 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride (40 mg base) with 200 mL water at 10:00: vasopressin range 1.14-1.88 pmol/L before and 2.46-9.16 at 2 hours (paired t test, one-tailed p = 0.006; about 0.012 two-tailed, editors' calculation), maximum between 1 and 2 hours, against a small decrease on 3 later untreated occasions (not compared statistically); sodium 139-145 mmol/L before and 140-142 at 2 hours, down 1-3 in 7 of 8 and up 1 in one (one-tailed p = 0.025; about 0.05 two-tailed, editors' calculation); urine not measured. Baggott et al. (2016), 1.5 mg/kg MDMA hydrochloride (1.26 mg/kg base) or placebo, double-blind, within person, sequence- and gender-balanced: Study 1 (16 people, 8 women; water limited to about 473 mL an hour; 1213 +/- 76 mL drunk in 8 hours, not differing by condition): maximum ADH by condition F(3,45) = 5.68, p = 0.002; prazosin alone z = 3.46 (p = 0.002), prazosin with MDMA z = 3.22 (p = 0.004), MDMA alone z = 1.21 (p = 0.589); minimum sodium by condition F(3,357) = 8.44 (p < 0.0001), MDMA alone t(357) = -4.05 (p < 0.0001), MDMA with prazosin t(357) = -3.50 (p = 0.0005), prazosin alone no effect; MDMA curves under 2 mmol/L below placebo at their lowest, around 3 hours (editors' approximate reading of Figure 3a). Study 2 (12 people, 6 women; 20 mL/kg water within 30 minutes, an hour after the capsule; two people who vomited in their MDMA sessions excluded): maximum ADH F(1,15) = 0.113 (p = 0.74), maximum copeptin F(1,9) = 0.019 (p = 0.89); minimum sodium F(1,9) = 13.2 (p = 0.005); means about 133.6 mmol/L at 3 hours after MDMA against about 137.7 after placebo, whose lowest mean was about 136 at 2 hours (editors' approximate readings of Figure 3b); one woman 127 mmol/L at 3 hours, transient, without symptoms. No mean, change or interval is printed for any sodium result. Urine pooled before dosing and over 0-8 and 8-24 hours; no urine result reported. Hysek et al. (2014), 32 healthy volunteers (16 women), 125 mg against placebo, double-blind crossover: copeptin before and 1 and 2 hours after not altered (no statistic printed). No study gives a frequency of difficulty passing urine.

risk_of_bias.note: The only evidence on passing urine is one case report (card sc_bryden_1995: JBI checklist, high risk for any statement about cause): the drug was never identified in the man or the tablets, the amount is his own account given in two stages, no bladder measurement or follow-up is reported, and no other cause was excluded beyond a normal examination. The hormone evidence comes from a before-and-after study with 3 untreated comparison occasions that were not compared statistically and one-tailed tests at one time point (card sc_henry_1998: ROBINS-I serious) and from a placebo-controlled study that collected urine and reported no urine result, was not registered and prints degrees of freedom that do not match the analyses described (card sc_baggott_2016: RoB 2 high).

inconsistency.note: No two studies measured passing urine, so there is nothing to be inconsistent on the claim's outcome. On the hormone, the uncontrolled study found a rise and the placebo-controlled studies found none (vasopressin and copeptin in Baggott et al., 2016; copeptin in Hysek et al., 2014); the statement reports both, and since the hormone is not the claim's outcome this is counted under indirectness, not again here.

indirectness.note: The controlled studies measured the hormone, copeptin and blood sodium, not difficulty passing urine, urine volume or bladder function, and none tested whether the hormone has anything to do with difficulty passing urine; they were done in healthy volunteers given one known dose by researchers. The case concerns one man and tablets of unknown content.

imprecision.note: One case; laboratory samples of 8, 16, 12 and 32 people, the water-load comparison resting on the 10 people with usable data from both sessions; no interval is printed for any hormone or sodium result, and the sodium sizes are read from figures.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable. A single case is published because it is unusual, which the statement respects by giving no frequency; the urine collected and not reported in Baggott et al. (2016) is rated under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: The only evidence on the claim's outcome, difficulty passing urine, is one case report: observational, starts low; down two levels for risk of bias, one for indirectness (the controlled studies measured a hormone and blood sodium, not passing urine) and one for imprecision; very low (the floor). Relation: insufficient evidence, because no study read measured how often passing urine becomes difficult after MDMA, or why. The placebo-controlled studies (Baggott et al., 2016; Hysek et al., 2014) would start high for their own outcomes, but they do not measure this claim's outcome and so do not raise it; their finding of no rise in the hormone or copeptin disagrees with the uncontrolled rise in 8 men (Henry et al., 1998), and the statement reports both without choosing an explanation. The alpha-adrenergic account is the case authors' reasoning, and no study read tested the hormone against urine; neither account is asserted. Status: single study (one case report on passing urine). Amounts appear only as each study's conditions, and the claim gives no advice on amounts or fluid.
